questions.q: What does a Key Lookup operator usually indicate, and what's the usual fix?
options: The table has no primary key defined
The database is running low on disk space
The query is using a deprecated join syntax
The nonclustered index used for the seek doesn't include all needed columns, forcing an extra trip per row to the clustered index; the fix is usually a covering index with those columns included
questions.explain: A Key Lookup fetches columns not present in the nonclustered index; adding them as INCLUDE columns lets the engine avoid the lookup entirely.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what makes a Sort operator (or Hash Match) dramatically worse than its baseline cost?
options: When it exceeds its memory grant and spills to tempdb, turning an in-memory operation into a disk-bound one
When the query has a WHERE clause at all
When the query runs during business hours
When the table has more than one index
questions.explain: A spill to tempdb, visible as a warning icon on the operator, means the operation ran out of its granted memory and had to finish the work on disk.

questions.q: Why can a Table/Index Scan on a large table be a red flag, per this lesson?
options: Scans indicate the database is corrupted
It does work proportional to the size of the entire table/index, which is wasteful when the query only actually needs a small subset of rows
Scans can only occur when there are zero indexes at all
Scans are always slower than Seeks in every possible case
questions.explain: A Scan reads the whole structure; against a 40-million-row table for a 200-row need, that's a large amount of unnecessary work, often pointing to a missing or unusable index.

questions.q: Why does WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2026 disable an index seek even if an index exists on OrderDate?
options: Wrapping the indexed column in a function makes the predicate non-seekable, so the optimizer can't use the index's B-tree to jump directly to matching rows
YEAR() is not a valid function in T-SQL
The index would need to be rebuilt daily to support this predicate
SQL Server never allows filtering on date columns
questions.explain: Applying a function to the indexed column obscures the direct relationship the optimizer needs to seek; rewriting as a range comparison (>= / <) restores seekability.

questions.q: Per this lesson, is a Hash Match operator automatically a performance problem?
options: Yes, Hash Match should always be avoided regardless of data size
No, because Hash Match never touches tempdb under any circumstance
Yes, because Hash Match can only be used with heaps, never with indexes
No — it's the optimizer's normal, often best choice for joining or aggregating large unsorted inputs; it becomes a problem mainly when it gets a bad memory grant and spills
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that none of these operators are automatically wrong — Hash Match is frequently the right choice, and the concern is specifically about memory grant problems and spills.
